one_line_reason: The only two records that directly assess dong quai (rather than folding it into a multi-herb TCM formula) both report no measurable benefit for its classic use (menopausal hot flashes), and neither gives the underlying trial's own PMID or dose.

selected.population: peri/menopausal women (systematic review, 30 RCTs of 19 different herbal interventions; dong quai evaluated in 2 of those RCTs)
selected.intervention: oral dong quai (Angelica sinensis) monotherapy for menopausal symptoms
selected.dose_as_stated: not stated (the review does not give the dong quai trials' own dose)
selected.why_selected: the most direct and recent (2026) evidence source; explicitly states the RCTs using dong quai (like black cohosh) found no measurable effect on menopausal symptoms, while other herbs in the same review did show benefit.

selected.population: men with prostate cancer undergoing androgen deprivation therapy (systematic review of hot-flash treatments, 35 studies)
selected.intervention: Dong Quai/Angelica Sinensis among several dietary supplements evaluated for treatment-induced hot flashes, oral
selected.primary_outcome: hot flash frequency and quality-of-life impact
selected.why_selected: a second, independent systematic review that also concludes dietary supplements including dong quai are ineffective for hot flashes, reinforcing the null/negative picture from an unrelated clinical population.

blockers: Neither review gives the underlying dong quai RCTs' own PMIDs, populations, or doses; central verification would first need to locate those two specific trials cited in 42451042 before any record could be built.

The only two direct assessments of dong quai both report no benefit (null/negative) for the classic consumer use case (vasomotor/hot flash symptoms), which weighs against building a positive-efficacy record from this literature.

Every other shortlisted record studies dong quai only as one ingredient among several in multi-herb Traditional Chinese Medicine formulas, or is a preclinical/mechanistic review, none of which isolate dong quai's own effect.

excluded_pmids.reason: Meta-analysis of multi-herb Chinese herbal medicine formulas (with standard treatment) for pediatric cerebral palsy; Angelica sinensis is one of several core herbs in combination prescriptions, not isolated.
Meta-analysis of TCM for chronic urticaria; Angelica sinensis is one of many frequently-used herbs across different multi-herb formulas, not isolated or dosed.
Meta-analysis of Chinese herbal FOOT BATHS (a topical soak, not an oral supplement) for diabetic foot; also a multi-herb combination, wrong route and wrong exposure.
Network meta-analysis of multi-herb TCM prescriptions combined with Western medicine for obesity-related PCOS; Angelica sinensis is one of several core herbs in various formulas, not isolated.
Preclinical (animal-model) meta-analysis of ligustilide, a compound found in Angelica sinensis, for ischemic stroke; not human evidence and not a whole-herb supplement.
Meta-analysis of multi-herb Chinese herbal medicine for postoperative ovarian endometriotic cysts; Angelica sinensis is one ingredient among many formula components.
Meta-analysis of multi-herb Chinese herbal medicine for antipsychotic-drug-induced amenorrhea; Angelica sinensis is one of several herbs in combination formulas.

Review of several different Chinese Herbal Medicines (including Angelica sinensis) for NK-cell immunomodulation in cancer; evidence is mostly extracts/formulas and cellular/animal studies, not an isolated dong quai human trial.

Narrative pharmacology review of Angelica sinensis for ischemic stroke, drawing mainly on preclinical studies and an injectable ('Angelica injection') preparation rather than an oral supplement human trial.
Systematic review of TCM effects on the Th17/Treg immune axis; Angelica sinensis appears as one of many herbs across different formulas and mechanistic studies, not isolated.
